A very common sentiment I'm hearing among math students: "I don't want to become a mathematician anymore." I've seen this before, I think the generation of digital artists who came of age around 2022 will be the last.

AI might not functionally replace mathematicians or artists, but it might well cause their near-extinction anyway, by crushing the spirits of the younger generations.

As models become more intelligent, without the right safeguards and monitoring they also become more dangerous. These issues are complex, thorny, and increasingly important for everyone to understand so that the world can weigh in and respond to rapidly escalating risks.

items.title: Do large language models actually understand the world, or are they just very good at pretending? Do...
items.content:
Do large language models actually understand the world, or are they just very good at pretending? Does it even matter?

Our recent special issue in the Royal Society, “World Models in Natural and Artificial Intelligence,” brings together pioneers across AI, biology, and philosophy to argue that the path to true intelligence runs through something deeper: the ability to model not just language, but causality, the self, and the physical world.

Featuring contributions from Douglas Hofstadter, Michael Levin, Josh Tenenbaum, Samuel Gershman, Melanie Mitchell, and others, the collection asks a radical question:

What if the next leap in AI requires not just more data, but systems that model themselves?

Here are 3 ideas that might redefine how we build AI:

1. Capability is not the same as true intelligence.

Current foundation models are incredibly capable, but they often lack true emergent intelligence. They learn surface statistics instead of compact, causal abstractions. Simply scaling compute will not fix this fundamental issue.

2. Self-modeling is an engineering primitive, not a philosophical luxury.

New research in the issue shows that when networks learn to predict their own internal states, they compress and simplify, becoming more efficient as a form of regularization. For physical AI and future agents, a self-model is what will allow them to adapt their own skills and morphologies in real-time.

3. The hardest problems in AI are continuous with the hardest problems of life.

Biological minds do not passively ingest data; they actively explore, driven by empowerment to increase control over their environment. If world modeling is about an agent representing itself in relation to its environment to survive and adapt, then general AI may need to look much more like artificial life.

The takeaway is that the next leap in AI won’t come from just scaling up next-token prediction, but rather from systems that are agentic, self-referential, and temporally grounded.

Read the introductory essay and the full special issue here: https://t.co/KnNJMiZ9lZ

What do you think is the most important missing ingredient in today’s AI systems?

items.title: OpenAI’s GPT Images 2.5 takes the top two spots on the Artificial Analysis Image Arena, generating h...
items.content:
OpenAI’s GPT Images 2.5 takes the top two spots on the Artificial Analysis Image Arena, generating higher quality images in less than half the time, while keeping the same price as GPT Image 2

Nearly five months after GPT Image 2’s release, OpenAI has released GPT Image 2.5 Flare and Sunburst. OpenAI positions Flare as the model choice for most applications, designed for everyday image generation at lower latency than GPT Image 2. Sunburst is positioned by OpenAI as offering higher quality for detailed creative work and tighter control across edits, but taking longer to generate images. Both models handle Text to Image and Image Editing.

Flare and Sunburst take the top two spots on both Artificial Analysis image leaderboards, with Flare #1 in Text to Image and Sunburst #1 in Image Editing. Our evaluation of both models was performed at “max” quality.

The largest gains were in Image Editing, with the biggest improvements over GPT Image 2 in:

➤ Composition & Framing: camera changes, zoom-outs and layout changes that must keep the scene intact, where Sunburst now holds the widest lead of any editing action.

➤ Text or Symbol Edits: changes to words, numbers, logos and symbols within an existing image, where Sunburst's gain over GPT Image 2 is second only to Composition & Framing.

These gains come at the same estimated output price as GPT Image 2 (high) for 1024 × 1024 images at the evaluated quality settings.

Both models are available through the OpenAI API. OpenAI has also released ChatGPT Images 2.5 in ChatGPT, ChatGPT Work, and Codex.

Congratulations to @OpenAI on the release!

See below for our analysis and example outputs of GPT Image 2.5 Flare and Sunburst in the Artificial Analysis Image Arena 🧵

items.title: We independently benchmarked Devin Fusion for its release today - this is the first time a multi-mod...
items.content:
We independently benchmarked Devin Fusion for its release today - this is the first time a multi-model coding agent has been included on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, and it effectively retains Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra performance while reducing costs

Devin Fusion runs a frontier lead model with a cost-efficient sidekick. We tested configurations from Cognition combining frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI with their new SWE-2 (medium) as a sidekick model. Configured with Claude Fable 5.1 (xhigh) + SWE-2 (medium), Devin Fusion scores 62 on the Coding Agent Index v1.5, while with GPT-6 Astra (xhigh) + SWE-2 (medium) it scores 59. The Fable configuration has the higher score, while the Astra configuration is 43% less expensive and completes tasks 31% faster.

Congratulations to @cognition on the release! See below for our results and analysis 🧵

items.title: Ling-3.0-flash-VL, Ant Group’s new flash tier open weights model, scores 25 on the Artificial Analys...
items.content:
Ling-3.0-flash-VL, Ant Group’s new flash tier open weights model, scores 25 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. At 124B total parameters 5.5B active parameters, it sits on the Intelligence vs. Active Parameter Pareto Frontier

@AntLingAGI has released Ling-3.0-flash-VL, an open weights reasoning model that adds image and video understanding to Ling-3.0-flash. Its mixture-of-experts architecture activates 5.5B of its 124B parameters per token, with support for a 256K token context window.

Key results:

➤ Ling-3.0-flash-VL sits on the Pareto Frontier for Intelligence vs. Active Parameters, scoring 25 with 5.5B active parameters. Among models with a similar total size, Qwen3.5 122B A10B (Reasoning) scores 16 and Mistral Medium 3.5 (high) scores 15.

➤ Ling-3.0-flash-VL features lower hallucination rate than comparable models, but with limited factual recall. Ling-3.0-flash-VL scores 14% on AA-Omniscience Accuracy and 22% on Hallucination Rate. Inkling Small answers more questions correctly at 33% Accuracy, but has a much higher Hallucination Rate at 63%.

➤ There remains room for improvement for difficult agentic tasks for Ling-3.0-flash-VL. The model scores 16% on AutomationBench-AA, which tests completing workflows across business apps while respecting guardrails, and 0% on Terminal-Bench v4.0, a harder terminal-use benchmark.

➤ Ling-3.0-flash-VL is decently verbose with its output. The model averages ~50k output tokens per Intelligence Index task vs. ~30k for Inkling Small (Reasoning), despite the similar overall scores. This will have cost implications for workloads with a high level of reasoning.

Additional model details:

➤ Type: Open weights reasoning model.

➤ Size: 124B total parameters, 5.5B active per token (MoE).

➤ Context window: 256K tokens.

➤ Modalities: Text, image, and video input; text output.

➤ API availability: First- and third-party APIs.

➤ License: MIT.

It's cool that there is more interest in eval tools!   

Some opportunities for improvement: 

1. Ri...
items.content:
It's cool that there is more interest in eval tools!   

Some opportunities for improvement: 

1. Right now, this workflow tries to quiz you up front about your recollection of your experience with a plugin.    It would be better if it was more "in-situ", meaning you could give feedback on the plugins as you are using them.

2. It goes off and builds datasets and judges automatically based on what you tell it in up front as well as what's documented in the plugin.  I would like to see it try to do error discovery with you first to allow you to annotate real traces / session history etc so you can figure out what's not working better.  

3. It was clunky to do this against a skill that wasn't a plugin.  I had to ask claude to set it up for me and it took 10 minutes to figure that out.  

4. I had to stare at the generated HTML for a while before I could understand what everything meant.  There is some onboarding experience that is missing but I'm not sure what that is yet.  

I'm sure this will get better over time and the things above seem doable.  It's also positive to see affordances for evals directly in our agents!
items.author: @HamelHusain
items.summary: Hamel Husain offers detailed constructive critique of a new plugin eval tool for Claude skills: feedback should be captured in-situ during use rather than via upfront quizzes; automatic dataset and judge generation should be preceded by collaborative error discovery on real traces; setup for non-plugin skills was clunky; and the generated HTML report lacks onboarding clarity.
items.reasoning: From a leading evals expert, this is original, technically deep practitioner feedback with solid engagement (146 likes, 16k views), though it critiques rather than announces and trails off mid-thought.
items.summary_html: Hamel Husain offers detailed constructive critique of a new plugin eval tool for Claude skills: feedback should be captured in-situ during use rather than via upfront quizzes; automatic dataset and judge generation should be preceded by collaborative error discovery on real traces; setup for non-plugin skills was clunky; and the generated HTML report lacks onboarding clarity.
items.content_html:
It's cool that there is more interest in eval tools!

Some opportunities for improvement:

1. Right now, this workflow tries to quiz you up front about your recollection of your experience with a plugin. It would be better if it was more "in-situ", meaning you could give feedback on the plugins as you are using them.

2. It goes off and builds datasets and judges automatically based on what you tell it in up front as well as what's documented in the plugin. I would like to see it try to do error discovery with you first to allow you to annotate real traces / session history etc so you can figure out what's not working better.

3. It was clunky to do this against a skill that wasn't a plugin. I had to ask claude to set it up for me and it took 10 minutes to figure that out.

4. I had to stare at the generated HTML for a while before I could understand what everything meant. There is some onboarding experience that is missing but I'm not sure what that is yet.

I'm sure this will get better over time and the things above seem doable. It's also positive to see affordances for evals directly in our agents!

Introducing the Automated AI Risk Outlook (AIRO): a dashboard of catastrophic risk forecasts from an ensemble of frontier AI models, updated weekly.

Current ensemble forecasts of an AI-related catastrophe that kills at least 10% of the global population:

• By 2030: 0.47%
• By 2050: 6%

This dashboard is a prototype, and forecasting catastrophic risk is extremely challenging. We see the current forecasts as tentative, but we expect them to improve over time as AI capabilities advance.

items.content_html:
@SethCronin Chess, go, and math are highly constrained, purely cognitive that allow exact simulation for games (and formal verification for math), and not in the open-ended physical world.

As I have been arguing for over a decade AI, AI techniques for the former are strong, for the latter they are weak. That remains true.

That said, we stupidly pushed the cognitive techniques without solving alignment. we should be extremely careful about doing the same in robotics.

items.title: There's something deeply philosophical about the importance of human understanding in a world where ...
items.content:
There's something deeply philosophical about the importance of human understanding in a world where most work is done by AI. 

Terence Tao's whole point in the letter isn't that AI is universally bad, but that it should be used in a way that complements the advancement of human understanding rather than doing work (like solving math proofs) for its own sake. 

You can obviously use AI to help accelerate research and understanding, but the point here is that you also don't have to in order to get things done. 

As someone who's largely optimistic about AI, I don't have concrete opinions on this matter yet, but I empathize with the broader question of how deeply humans should strive to understand the world vs. fully offloading it to others.

One of the main issues with AI document parsing is that because no solution is 100% accuracy, it's hard to tell if a given page is parsed incorrectly: for instance a misaligned table, missing/hallucinated values, or messy scans 

over the past few months we've invested a lot in models that provide more calibrated confidence scores - it will give you a confidence level that the page is parsed correctly. it is correlated with the parsing mode and how complex the source page is. 

this allows you to bake in human-in-the-loop mechanisms where you can review and correct the outputs, or trigger automated fallback logic, for highly sensitive paperwork-heavy processes.

Generating a nice-l...
items.content:
I've been trying Codex to analyze a dataset, and honestly, I've gotten nowhere.

Generating a nice-looking report about the data isn't enough.

For this to be useful, Codex needs to inspect tables, clean existing data, choose the correct statistical methods, run the analysis, and support its conclusions with evidence.

There are too many tasks to coordinate, and it's taking me a long time to write a skill with the complete workflow so I can keep Codex on task.

The Apodex team reached out to me to show me their Apodex 1.1 model. It includes an open-source framework and an open-weight version of the model.

I uploaded a CSV file and asked a question that I couldn't answer by simply summarizing the table.

Apodex created an analysis plan, wrote the code, and executed it inside a single long-running task:

1. It inspected the tables
2. It determined the steps to answer the question
3. It wrote Python code to clean and transform the dataset
4. It executed the scripts in its environment
5. It generated a final report with the answer

This is what Apodex calls Environment Scaling.

I could intervene while a task was running, and the system preserved all intermediate results that remained valid and replanned only the affected parts instead of restarting the task.

Apodex 1.1 takes reasoning out of the report and puts it into executing real tasks.

Thanks to the team for collaborating with me on this post.

items.title: Devin Fusion performs well for cost efficiency and performance, and currently sits on the Pareto fro...
items.content:
Devin Fusion performs well for cost efficiency and performance, and currently sits on the Pareto frontier for Coding Agent Index score vs. Cost per Task in both configurations we tested

Devin Fusion CLI with Claude Fable 5.1 (xhigh) + SWE-2 (medium) scores 61.7 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index v1.5. This is almost tied with Claude Fable 5.1 (max, with fallback) in Claude Code at 62.2 despite the lower effort, and costs 36% less at $7.9 per task for the Fusion configuration vs. $12.4 for Claude Code. Speed is also essentially flat, with time per task of 35.8 vs. 34.8 minutes.

This pattern holds across the underlying evaluations: Fusion scores 63.1 vs. 64.3 on DeepSWE 1.1, 65.9 vs. 64.8 on SWE-Atlas QnA, and 56.1 vs. 57.6 on Terminal-Bench 4.0.

This means that OpenAI’s image models currently lead every single Text to Image capability and use case we measure.

items.title:
Google's new paper proved your skill file matters least in training

Hand-writing agent instructions...
items.content:
Google's new paper proved your skill file matters least in training

Hand-writing agent instructions is a losing game. Files rot the moment tasks shift.

Skill evolution rewrites them from rollout evidence instead. But most loops forget every failure.

Their WikiSkill setup keeps a private notebook behind the skills. So the coach learns from history while the actor stays blind.

> Blind the rollout actor
> Log every rejected edit
> Quarantine every transferred skill

The notebook lifted accuracy 48.7 to 63.7 Then peeking dropped it back to 60.9

And transferred skills beat self-made ones 70.2 to 63.4, Yet one crashed a stronger model 50.5 to 18.1

Small models can discover skills that bigger ones execute. EvoSkill's repo is public under Apache 2.0

So gate every skill like a model release

Full breakdown ↓↓ 
The appendix builds the loop in an hour
items.author: @AlphaSignalAI
items.summary: AlphaSignalAI summarizes a Google paper on skill evolution for agents (WikiSkill/EvoSkill): hand-written agent instruction files rot as tasks shift, and skills can instead be rewritten from rollout evidence. Conclusion: gate every skill like a model release; repo is public under Apache 2.0.

We also see some risks associated with relying on automated AI forecasts of catastrophic risk:

1) A...
items.content:
We also see some risks associated with relying on automated AI forecasts of catastrophic risk:

1) As evidence of AI model deception emerges, AI forecasts may be influenced by strategic behavior: a highly capable but misaligned model trying to evade human suspicion may lower its estimates to avoid causing alarm. This “sandbagging” behavior may also arise if companies, concerned about regulation or other threats to profit, intentionally post-train models to underplay the risk of AI-caused harms.

2) Now that these forecasts are published, they will enter future models’ training corpora, potentially making them self-reinforcing.

We are currently developing benchmarks that better help us aggregate forecasts, and, where possible detect and counteract the risks we identify above.

items.title: We also ask LLMs how the risk of an AI-related catastrophe changes depending on AI capabilities. Mod...
items.content:
We also ask LLMs how the risk of an AI-related catastrophe changes depending on AI capabilities. Models forecast the frontier score on the Epoch Capabilities Index (ECI) six months from now, then forecast risk outcomes conditional on frontier models achieving higher- or lower-than-median scores.

As of September 10, the median forecast for frontier ECI on March 10, 2027, was 176. When each model instead assumed its own 75th-percentile ECI outcome, its forecast of an AI-related catastrophe by 2030 rose by an ensemble factor of 1.42 relative to its unconditional forecast.

Flare pairs its quality gains with a much shorter wait for images and edits, with GPT Image 2.5 Flare (max) having a ~63% faster latency than GPT Image 2 (high)

In our independent inference speed benchmarking, our preliminary results show similar improvements to OpenAI's claim of 50% lower latency for Flare versus GPT Image 2:

➤ Flare (max) reduced median generation time by 63%, from 142.9 to 52.7 seconds

➤ Sunburst (max) reduced median generation time by 24% to 108.9s

Our testing used 1024 × 1024 PNG outputs and represents a median across several testing runs including inference and image transfer.

In Image Editing, GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst sets the frontier in 6 of 7 editing actions and 8 of 10 use cases

Our Image Editing arena scores models on two axes: seven editing actions which represent what an edit asks the model to do, and the same ten use cases as Text to Image.

Sunburst's largest leads over the next-best model are in Composition & Framing and Object-Level Edit, both over GPT Image 2 (high), and Text or Symbol Edits, over Microsoft's MAI-Image-2.6. Sunburst closely trails Microsoft's MAI-Image-2.5-Pro in Enhancement & Restoration, the one editing action it does not lead.

➤ Composition & Framing covers camera changes, zoom-outs, and layout changes that must preserve the scene or design.

➤ Object-Level Edit covers adding, removing, replacing, or changing individual objects within an image.

➤ Text or Symbol Edits covers changes to words, numbers, logos, and symbols within an existing image.

items.content:
The accompanying white paper explores preliminary forecasts of how AI risk mitigation policies change the probability of catastrophic outcomes.

We tested six individual policy scenarios, a combined package, and a no-new-policy baseline, adapted from an upcoming LEAP survey wave.

Among the individual scenarios, the policies that most reduce AI risk by 2030 and 2050, according to the models’ forecasts, are:

• A compute cap on frontier AI R&D in the U.S. and China
• A binding requirement that frontier AI models be vetted by an international body before release

We plan to add policy conditions to the main AIRO dashboard in a future update. For preliminary analyses, see the white paper linked below, which includes definitions of each policy. Our policy forecasts focus on catastrophic risk and do not explore other potential costs and benefits of each policy.

https://t.co/7MsApFktyS

items.title: AIRO currently puts the probability of an AI-related catastrophe that kills at least 10% of the glob...
items.content:
AIRO currently puts the probability of an AI-related catastrophe that kills at least 10% of the global population at 0.47% by 2030 and 6% by 2050.

For comparison, domain experts gave probabilities of 0.3% by 2030 and 2% by 2050 on a similar question in our Longitudinal Expert AI Panel (LEAP) in May–June 2026.

AIRO also collects forecasts at shorter and longer time horizons: from six months to 2100. We highlight these estimates to show cumulative risk over time, but long-term forecasting is very difficult. We will gather evidence on how quickly LLM forecasting accuracy degrades for predictions farther into the future.

items.title:
Production traffic is not uniform.

You get a few requests that need your best model, but most are s...
items.content:
Production traffic is not uniform.

You get a few requests that need your best model, but most are simple questions and lookups you can solve with cheaper, faster models.

The most expensive mistake you can make today is sending every request to your strongest model.

You need routing. Period.

This is the simplest trick to improve the architecture of whatever you are building.

Please, don't implement routing yourself. You don't have to.

I'm currently working with TrueFoundry's Auto Routing. It reads each request, classifies it as simple, medium, or complex, and sends it to the model assigned to that tier.

You have two choices:

1. Send every request to the free heuristic classifier to score signals such as technical vocabulary, code, prompt length, and multi-step reasoning.

2. Send the request to an LLM classifier when its difficulty requires a more nuanced judgment.

The beauty of using routing is that nothing changes in your code. You still call a single endpoint model, but routing works behind the scenes to pair every request with the best possible model.

TrueFoundry ran several experiments with two different setups:

1. Send every request to Claude Opus
2. Send every request to a router with Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus

The first experiment ran 550 deterministically graded academic prompts through every setup. Auto Routing was 69% cheaper while retaining 98% of the baseline quality.

The second experiment ran three production-shaped workloads through every setup, using user chats, developer chats, and long agent tasks. Auto Routing was 80% cheaper.

Thanks to the TrueFoundry team for partnering with me on this post.

Our Text to Image arena scores models on two axes: nine capabilities, which are the skills that go into making an image, and ten use cases, which measure how those capabilities combine in real workloads.

➤ Knowledge covers real landmarks, species, and domain facts across science and common sense.

➤ Material covers surface properties, transparency, subsurface scattering, and texture realism.

➤ Physics covers gravity, support, collision, and thermal and state change.

items.title:
How AIRO works:

• We select the four highest-scoring eligible models on the ECI, keeping one model ...
items.content:
How AIRO works:

• We select the four highest-scoring eligible models on the ECI, keeping one model per family.
• We ask them forecasting questions drawn from our work on catastrophic risk, eliciting forecasts at multiple time horizons and severity thresholds.
• Each model answers all questions in one forecasting session, conducting its own research via an agentic harness (with web-search and page-reading tools.)
• After at least 10 research-tool calls, models submit their forecasts along with a short rationale and a list of key sources.
• We report the four models' forecasts alongside their unweighted median.

items.title: When I started to build ChapterPal last year, I spent about a day adding a new paper (this involves ...
items.content:
When I started to build ChapterPal last year, I spent about a day adding a new paper (this involves either conversion from LaTeX to Markdown or OCR when LaTeX is unavailable) and about a week adding a textbook.

Today, I add about 20 papers and 2 textbooks a day (both, not either/or). And I keep adding new UX features every day.

And I still feel that I'm not productive enough. And it's not just a feeling. I have about 95,000 papers in the pipeline and nearly 2,000 textbooks.

With the current level of productivity, adding all of them in good quality will take years. I don't have years to spend on this, I cannot clone myself, and I don't have money, nor do I want to hire people.

I need better AI.

items.content:
AIRO also tracks AI-related human-caused epidemics. The ensemble gives a 13% probability that incidents beginning from September 10, 2026, through 2050 cumulatively reach 100,000 deaths (or equivalent morbidity) OR $220 billion in damages. This is not a forecast of deaths alone; it includes mortality, morbidity, and economic damages.

Across the four models, forecasts range from 6% (GPT–5.5 Pro) to 19% (GPT–6 Astra).

items.title:
Why use AI models to forecast catastrophic risk?

• Models don't get fatigued, so we can elicit many...
items.content:
Why use AI models to forecast catastrophic risk?

• Models don't get fatigued, so we can elicit many forecasts across time horizons and scenarios, and reforecast as new information arrives, tracking how forecasts change.
• AI models have likely already achieved parity with superforecasters on ForecastBench, our forecasting accuracy benchmark, and will continue to improve over time.
• Evidence from simulated worlds shows us that AI accuracy at forecasting rare events improves with model capabilities.

AIRO runs weekly, so forecasts of catastrophic risk update as the world and AI capabilities change.

ForecastBench: https://t.co/x0D8iLbhvY

Now you can learn calculus on your own on @ChapterPal from this gem of a textbook: "Active Calculus (2nd Edition)" by Matthew Boelkins (2025).

The book has hundreds of illustrations and interactive exercises. ChapterPal adds to these on-demand understanding control quizzes and tutoring.

items.title:
AIRO is still a work in progress. Our potential next steps include:

• Enabling top AI forecasting c...
items.content:
AIRO is still a work in progress. Our potential next steps include:

• Enabling top AI forecasting companies and other researchers to submit their AI forecasting models to the dashboard. We will prioritize displaying models that show accuracy on relevant benchmarks.
• Generating forecasts on "cruxes"—key intermediate indicators related to catastrophic risk forecasts.
• Adding model rationales and explanations of forecast changes to the dashboard.
• Validating and extending the dashboard by refining ensemble forecasts and using a larger set of intermediate questions related to catastrophic outcomes.
• Adding conditional forecasts to understand the impacts of proposed mitigation policies on AI risk.
• Having a range of AI forecaster personas—some more "concerned" about AI catastrophic risk, and some more "skeptical"—provide competing forecasts on a wide selection of intermediate questions, to assess which perspectives are most accurate over time.

If you have ideas or questions about improving AIRO, please email info@forecastingresearch.org
items.author: @Research_FRI
items.summary: FRI outlines AIRO's roadmap: letting AI forecasting companies submit models for the dashboard, generating forecasts on intermediate crux indicators of catastrophic risk, adding model rationales, refining ensembles with more intermediate questions, adding conditional policy forecasts, and running competing concerned-vs-skeptical forecaster personas to assess which perspectives prove most accurate.
items.reasoning: Thoughtful research roadmap from a credible institution, though incremental to the main launch post and with minimal engagement.
